blocks.text: Until 1934, most people in Turkey had no surname. You were known by your first name and, when that wasn't enough, by something added to it: your father's name, your trade, your home town or a nickname. Some families were known by a name ending in *-oğlu* (son of) or in the Persian *-zade* (born of).

The Surname Law (*Soyadı Kanunu*) was adopted on 21 June 1934, published on 2 July and came into force on 2 January 1935. Every family had to choose a surname and register it, and people who had not chosen one within two years faced penalties. The law ruled out surnames taken from military ranks or official titles, from the names of tribes or of foreign races and nations, and names that were offensive or ridiculous; the Persian *-zade* was dropped too.

Many families chose a word for a quality, or for something solid and lasting: *Yılmaz* (undaunted), *Kaya* (rock), *Demir* (iron), *Çelik* (steel), *Yıldız* (star), *Şahin* (hawk). Others took their trade or their place of origin. Today *Yılmaz*, *Kaya* and *Demir* are the three most common surnames in Turkey.

In November 1934, two more laws followed. One abolished titles such as *ağa*, *hacı*, *hafız*, *efendi*, *bey* and *paşa* in official use. The other gave Mustafa Kemal the surname *Atatürk*, father of the Turks, and reserved it for him alone.

In everyday speech, though, *Bey* and *Hanım* never went away. Placed after the first name, *Mehmet Bey* and *Ayşe Hanım* are still the usual polite way to address a colleague, a neighbour or a shopkeeper, and you'll use them throughout this course.

Because the law banned foreign suffixes and the names of other nations, it also affected families from Turkey's minorities, among them Armenians, Greeks, Jews, Assyrians and Kurds, many of whom adopted Turkish-sounding surnames. Historians discuss the law as part of the early Republic's effort to build a single national identity.

blocks.title: The word itself
blocks.text: The Turkish for surname is *soyadı*, from *soy* (lineage, family line) and *ad* (name). An official form asks for *Adı* and *Soyadı*: first name and surname.
Here is how two people with brand-new surnames might have introduced themselves in 1935, in the Turkish you know from this unit:

lines.en: Hello, I'm Ayşe Yılmaz. I'm a teacher.

lines.tr: Memnun oldum, Ayşe Hanım. Ben Mehmet Demir, mühendisim.
lines.en: Nice to meet you, Ayşe. I'm Mehmet Demir, an engineer.
